topics.chapterTitle: Understanding Atomics and the C++ Memory Model
topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: Atomics prevent certain conflicting accesses from becoming data races and provide ordering tools for communication. They do not make an entire algorithm correct merely by replacing int with atomic<int>. This chapter separates a relaxed statistics counter from release-acquire publication of ordinary data, then explains why ordering, lifetime, and logical ownership must be reasoned about together.

blocks.text: A counter becomes atomic and the program stops losing increments. The developer then replaces every mutex with atomic flags and assumes the larger data structure is safe. Its nodes can still be destroyed while another thread reads them, and two fields can still describe incompatible states. Atomic access to one object is a local property, not a complete concurrent algorithm.

blocks.text: This chapter separates atomicity, ordering, notification, and lifetime. A relaxed counter needs indivisible updates but no publication of associated payload. A one-shot handoff needs a release/acquire relationship connecting the writer’s ordinary payload update to the reader’s later access. Neither example solves reusable queues, lock-free reclamation, or every possible startup and shutdown failure.

blocks.text: Loads and stores access one atomic value. A load can request an ordering appropriate to the reader; a store can request an ordering appropriate to the writer. Not every ordering is valid for every operation. Use the documented combinations rather than passing a memory-order enum selected by a generic “stronger is always safer” rule without understanding the operation.

blocks.text: Atomic types are not universally lock-free. The implementation can use internal locking for some sizes and platforms. is_lock_free reports a property of the relevant implementation or object; is_always_lock_free expresses a compile-time guarantee for the specialization when true. A false result does not make the operation non-atomic. A true result does not establish that the entire application is lock-free or bounded in latency.

blocks.text: Initialization and destruction still require ownership. An atomic object cannot safely be destroyed while another thread may access it, and publishing a pointer to an incompletely initialized owner is not repaired by making one member atomic. Place shared state in a lifetime that encloses every accessing thread, then use synchronization to govern the accesses during that lifetime.

topics.title: 20.1.2 Performing Read-Modify-Write Operations
topics.summary: Operations such as fetch_add atomically read a value, compute an update, and return the prior value under one modification. A separate load followed by store is not equivalent when several threads update concurrently; intervening updates can be lost. Compare-exchange supports conditional updates but requires a carefully designed retry and failure-order policy.

blocks.text: A counter can use relaxed ordering when only the counter’s own value matters and another synchronization event establishes when final observation occurs. blocks.text: Read-modify-write operations combine reading the previous value and storing a new value as one atomic operation. fetch_add returns the old value while applying the increment; compare-exchange conditionally replaces a value according to whether it matches the expected state. These primitives can express counters, ticket assignment, and more complex algorithms, but each algorithm still needs an invariant and progress argument.

blocks.text: A relaxed fetch-add is appropriate for the chapter’s independent event counter. Each increment must be counted without loss, but no associated non-atomic payload is being published through that increment. After joining both workers, the supervisor can read the final count and compare it with the known number of operations. The join supplies the completion boundary; relaxed does not mean “the final result may randomly be wrong.”

blocks.text: A check followed by a separate increment is not equivalent to a conditional atomic update. Two threads can both observe capacity before either increments. Use an appropriate compare-exchange loop or a lock protecting the complete reservation transition when the invariant requires “increment only if below a limit.” The simpler operation may be safer and easier to verify than a custom lock-free loop.

blocks.text: Compare-exchange updates its expected argument when comparison fails, and weak compare-exchange can fail spuriously. A retry loop must incorporate the new observed state and preserve the algorithm’s validity across repeated attempts. Side effects performed inside the retry loop can be repeated; do not send messages or modify unrelated state as though the body will execute exactly once.

blocks.text: Counter wrap, ABA, and reclamation are separate obligations. A value can change from A to B and back to A while another thread is paused; equality of the final bits does not prove nothing happened. A pointer can be removed and its storage reused while another thread retains a stale observation. Generation tags help some identity problems but do not by themselves keep objects alive. These advanced issues are why the chapter stops short of presenting a casual lock-free linked structure.

topics.title: 20.2.1 Understanding Acquire and Release Semantics
topics.summary: A release operation can publish preceding writes when an acquire operation observes the appropriate released value under the memory model’s rules. In a one-shot ready flag, the producer writes ordinary payload data and then stores true with release; a consumer that observes true with acquire can read the published payload after that synchronization.

blocks.text: The one-shot restriction is important. After publication, the producer does not overwrite the payload while the consumer reads it. topics.title: 20.2.2 Understanding Sequential and Relaxed Ordering
topics.summary: Sequentially consistent operations provide an additional global ordering framework for those operations, while relaxed operations provide atomicity and modification-order guarantees without the same cross-object ordering. The default atomic operations commonly use sequential consistency unless a different order is supplied.

topics.title: Failure clinic — An atomic flag around a data race
topics.summary: A writer stores a new payload repeatedly and toggles a ready flag. The reader sees ready, starts reading, and the writer begins the next update. The flag is atomic, but the payload accesses overlap without the required ownership handoff. Introduce an acknowledgement, double-buffer ownership protocol, queue, or lock that prevents reuse while the reader still owns access.

Create a small startup-failure model in which the consumer construction is rejected after the finite producer starts. Verify that the producer can complete and be joined without waiting for missing work. A separate queue exercise should show why producer-first alone is insufficient when the producer can block on capacity.

Review a proposed atomic reservation counter. Determine whether a separate load and increment can exceed capacity, then specify the invariant a compare-exchange loop or mutex must maintain. Include the behavior at capacity and at the numeric limit, not only the successful reservation path.

Review reasoning. Does atomicity of one field make a whole struct transactionally consistent? No. Does relaxed mean updates may be lost? No, not for the atomic read-modify-write used here. Does notify publish ordinary payload data by itself? No. Does release/acquire allow the producer to overwrite a payload still being read? No. Does a successful stress test prove every allowed schedule correct? No.

Completion criterion. Deliver an object-lifetime argument and a happens-before diagram for each shared-data path. Every memory-order choice should have a stated purpose, and every waiter should retain a reachable completion or cancellation transition even during partial startup failure.
